free.title: Socrates Sculpture Park
free.caption:
FREE · LONG ISLAND CITY

A free sculpture park on the Long Island City waterfront, and most New Yorkers have still never crossed the river for it. Socrates Sculpture Park is four acres of East River shoreline where artists build the work outdoors, in public, instead of shipping it in finished.

It started in 1986 as an illegal dumping site that artists cleared themselves, and it has never charged admission. On view now is Homecoming: Chakaia Booker, a returning fellow shown as part of the park's 40th anniversary year. The skyline across the water is Roosevelt Island and Midtown, and the lawn is the seat for it.

One Labor Day catch: the park closes at 1PM today instead of sunset, so this is a morning trip.

Save it, then send it to the friend who swears everything in this city costs money now.

📷 Socrates Sculpture Park

food.title: Joe's Pizza
food.caption:
CHEAP EATS · GREENWICH VILLAGE

Cheap eats in NYC still start with a slice, and Joe's Pizza on Carmine Street is the one the whole city measures the rest against. Joe Pozzuoli came from Naples and opened it in 1975. He is still the owner, and it is still family run.

There are four Manhattan counters now: 7 Carmine St in Greenwich Village, 150 East 14th St, 124 Fulton St downtown, and 1435 Broadway in Times Square. Carmine Street is the original corner and the one worth the walk.

It is a stand-up shop, not a restaurant. Order at the counter, take the paper plate, eat at the ledge or on the sidewalk like everyone else.

One move that changes it: ask for the slice reheated instead of taking it straight off the tray.

Save this for the next time someone tells you there is nothing left to eat downtown under fifteen dollars.

📷 Joe's Pizza

art.title: 6 Secrets of Roosevelt Island
art.caption:
HIDDEN GEM · ROOSEVELT ISLAND

Roosevelt Island is two miles of NYC that most residents only ever see from a car window on the Queensboro Bridge, and it is free to walk end to end. Six things hiding on it:

The lighthouse on the north tip was built in 1872 by James Renwick Jr., who also designed St. Patrick's Cathedral. It was relit in 2022 for its 150th year.

The red tram opened in 1976 as a stopgap while the subway was built, then stayed. It was the first aerial tramway in North America used for commuter transit, and it takes a normal fare.

Blackwell House dates to about 1796, one of the few post-Revolution farmhouses left in the city. The island runs on an underground vacuum that pulls 5.8 tons of trash a day at 70 mph, so there are no garbage trucks. Four Freedoms Park is Louis Kahn's only New York building, finished in 2012, decades after his death. The visitor center is a 1909 trolley kiosk with a Guastavino tile ceiling.

Ride the tram over, not the F train. It costs the same and the view does not.

📷 Roosevelt Island Tramway
